title: The Battle of Verdun
subject: histoire
description: For **299 days**, French and German armies tore each other apart around Verdun. **700,000** casualties for almost no ground gained: the symbol of the horror of the trenches.

hero.hook: 299 days for a few kilometers of mud, and 700,000 soldiers out of the fight.

blocks.text: In **1916**, for **299 days**, French and German troops fought over a few square kilometers around **Verdun**, a fortress town in eastern France. This was no brilliant breakthrough. It was a battle of attrition, with about **700,000** men killed or wounded.
Verdun became the symbol of the horror of the trenches. Decades later, it became the symbol of Franco-German reconciliation as well.

sections.title: The German plan: bleed France dry

blocks.text: Since 1914 the Western Front had frozen into [[Trench warfare]]: lines of ditches running from the North Sea to Switzerland. The German general **Erich von Falkenhayn** wanted to “bleed France white.” He picked Verdun, a place Paris could not give up without losing face. The operation was code named [[Gericht]], German for “the court.”

blocks.caption: The trenches of Verdun: a landscape eaten away by artillery

blocks.text: The opening bombardment of **February 21, 1916** was so violent that it was heard in the Vosges, more than **150 km** away.

On **February 21**, **1,200 guns** pounded the French lines. On the **25th**, **Fort Douaumont**, the key to the whole defense, fell almost without a fight. From then on Paris had to stake everything on Verdun: the trap set by Falkenhayn was working.

sections.title: Pétain, the Sacred Way and the rotation of troops

blocks.text: General **Philippe Pétain** organized the survival of the sector. The **Sacred Way** linked [[Bar-le-Duc]], a town behind the lines, to Verdun: nearly **6,000 trucks** a day, one vehicle every **14 seconds**. When a truck broke down, it was shoved into the ditch so the road stayed open.

blocks.caption: The Sacred Way, the vital supply artery of the French army

blocks.text: With the [[Noria]] system, Pétain rotated his divisions fast: a unit spent a short spell at the front, then was relieved. As a result, about **70%** of the French army fought at Verdun at one moment or another. The battle became a national experience.

sections.title: The hell of the guns, for almost nothing

blocks.text: In the summer, the [[Battle of the Somme (1916)]], a Franco-British offensive further north, took pressure off Verdun. Under General **Robert Nivelle**, the French retook Douaumont and then Fort Vaux. The battle ended on **December 18, 1916**. The lines had barely moved.
Fleury-devant-Douaumont was taken and retaken **16 times** in two months, then wiped off the map. It is one of the “villages that died for France”, still administered even though nobody lives there.

About **370,000** French and **330,000** German soldiers were killed or maimed. The [[heavy artillery of the Great War]] killed far more men than hand to hand fighting ever did. [[Red Zones]] remain unfit for any civilian life: too much unexploded ordnance, too much poisoned soil.

sections.title: From the ossuary to the handshake

blocks.text: The **Douaumont Ossuary** (1932) holds the remains of **130,000** French and German soldiers, mixed together. On **September 22, 1984**, French president **François Mitterrand** and German chancellor **Helmut Kohl** held hands in front of the monument. Verdun became a symbol of European peace.

blocks.text: **Verdun** (**1916**): **299** days of industrial war, about **700,000** casualties for no ground gained, and later the symbol of Franco-German reconciliation.
